summary: This standards-track memo defines the Management Information Base (MIB) objects used to monitor and manage TCP implementations through SNMP. It works for both IPv4 and IPv6. It replaces earlier TCP MIB definitions, including RFC 2452 and RFC 2012.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines the counters and tables that a network manager reads over SNMP to find out what a machine's TCP connections are doing. It covers both IPv4 and IPv6, and it keeps open connections and listening ports in separate tables because they behave differently.

questions: how to monitor tcp connections with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP objects a manager reads to see what a device's TCP stack is doing, in one table for both IPv4 and IPv6.

tldr.problem: Network managers need to see what a device's TCP stack is doing: how many connections are open, which ports are listening, and whether packets are being lost or reset. Earlier TCP MIBs only covered IPv4 and mixed connections together with listening sockets.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4022 defines one TCP MIB module with a group of counters, a connection table and a separate listener table. Addresses use the version-neutral InetAddress type, so one set of objects covers IPv4 and IPv6.
tldr.outcome: A manager can list every connection with its state and owning process, and can end a connection by writing one value. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2452 and RFC 2012 and is a Proposed Standard from March 2005 that has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4022 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2005. It obsoletes RFC 2452 and RFC 2012, and it has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: What a MIB Is
sections.content:
Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, termed the Management Information Base or MIB. MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms defined in the Structure of Management Information (SMI).

This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. In practice a MIB module is a document that names objects, gives each one a number in a tree of numbers, and says what each object contains and who may read or change it. A manager on the network asks a device for those numbers and gets the values back.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is a shared list of named readings, each with a number, that a manager can ask a device for over SNMP. This document says which readings about TCP exist and what they mean.

sections.title: What the Module Contains
sections.content:
The TCP MIB consists of two tables and a group of scalars.

The tcp group of scalars includes two sets of objects. The first covers parameters of a TCP protocol engine, such as the retransmission algorithm in use, for example Van Jacobson's algorithm, and the retransmission timeout values. The second covers statistics of a TCP protocol engine, with counters for the number of active and passive opens, input and output segments, and errors. Discontinuities in the statistics are identified via the sysUpTime object, so a reader can tell when a counter was reset.

The tcpConnectionTable provides access to status information for all TCP connections handled by a TCP protocol engine, and it also reports the identification of the operating system level processes that handle those connections. The tcpListenerTable provides access to information about all TCP listening endpoints known by the engine, and it likewise reports the operating system processes behind them.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three parts: a set of counters and settings for the whole TCP stack, a table of current connections, and a table of ports the device is listening on.

sections.title: Why the Old Table Was Dropped
sections.content:
TCP related MIB objects were originally defined as part of the RFC1213-MIB defined in RFC 1213. The TCP related objects were later copied into a separate MIB module and published in RFC 2012 in SMIv2 format.

Both earlier versions of the TCP MIB defined the tcpConnTable, which was deprecated for two reasons. First, it only supports IPv4. The current approach in the IETF is to write IP version neutral MIBs, based on the InetAddressType and InetAddress constructs defined in RFC 4001, rather than having separate definitions for each version of IP. This reduces the overhead when new objects are introduced, since there is only one place to add them, so the approach of RFC 2452 with separate tables is not continued.

Second, the old table mixed listening endpoints with connections. Connections tend to have a different behaviour and management access pattern than listening endpoints, so splitting the original table into two allows specific status and statistics objects to be added for each.

As a result the IPV6-TCP-MIB defined in RFC 2452 was moved to Historic status, because the approach of having separate IP version specific tables is no longer followed. Implementation of RFC 2452 is no longer suggested. The old tcpConnTable is kept in this module with the status deprecated, in favour of the version neutral table.
sections.plainLanguage: The previous table only understood IPv4 and put listening sockets in with live connections, even though the two are managed differently. Splitting them and using one address type for both IP versions fixes both problems, so the older IPv6-only MIB was retired.

sections.title: The Connection Table
sections.content:
The tcpConnectionTable holds one row per current TCP connection. Each row is transient: it ceases to exist when, or soon after, the connection makes the transition to the CLOSED state. Unlike earlier TCP MIBs, there is a separate table for connections in the LISTEN state.

A row is indexed by six columns: the local address type, the local address, the local port, the remote address type, the remote address and the remote port. The address columns use the InetAddress type, and the port columns use InetPortNumber, which is why the same table serves IPv4 and IPv6. The RFC warns implementors not to create entries that would result in OIDs with more than 128 subidentifiers, otherwise the information cannot be accessed by SNMPv1, SNMPv2c or SNMPv3.

Two further columns complete the row. tcpConnectionState holds the state of the connection and is read-write. tcpConnectionProcess holds the system's process ID for the process associated with the connection, or zero if there is no such process, and is expected to be the same as the hrSWRunIndex of the HOST-RESOURCES-MIB or the sysApplElmtRunIndex of the SYSAPPL-MIB for some row in the appropriate tables. That lets a management application group connections by the program that owns them.
sections.plainLanguage: Each row is one live connection, identified by its two addresses and two ports. The row also says which state the connection is in and which program on the device is using it.

sections.title: States and Ending a Connection
sections.content:
The tcpConnectionState object holds an integer from a fixed list of TCP states: closed(1), listen(2), synSent(3), synReceived(4), established(5), finWait1(6), finWait2(7), closeWait(8), lastAck(9), closing(10), timeWait(11) and deleteTCB(12). The value listen(2) is included only for parallelism to the old table and should not be used, because a connection in the LISTEN state belongs in the listener table instead.

The only value that may be set by a management station is deleteTCB(12). It is therefore appropriate for an agent to return a badValue response if a management station attempts to set the object to any other value. When a management station sets the object to deleteTCB(12), the TCB, as defined in RFC 793, of the corresponding connection on the managed node is deleted, which results in immediate termination of the connection. As an implementation-specific option, a RST segment may be sent from the managed node to the other TCP endpoint, although RST segments are not sent reliably.
sections.plainLanguage: The state column lists the familiar TCP states. A manager may read it, but the only thing it may write is a request to drop the connection, which deletes the TCP control block on the device and ends the connection at once.

sections.title: The Listener Table and Conformance
sections.content:
The tcpListenerTable holds one row per TCP listening endpoint, indexed by the local address type, the local address and the local port. The RFC describes three ways a listening application can be represented. An application willing to accept both IPv4 and IPv6 datagrams is represented by an address type of unknown (0) and an address of a zero-length octet string. An application willing to accept only IPv4 or only IPv6 is represented by the appropriate address type and the address 0.0.0.0 or :: respectively. An application listening for data destined only to a specific IP address is represented by the appropriate address type with that specific local address. The address type in this table represents the address type used for the communication, irrespective of the higher-layer abstraction.

The tcpListenerProcess column carries the process ID for the process associated with the listener, or zero if there is no such process, using the same HOST-RESOURCES-MIB and SYSAPPL-MIB values as the connection table.

The module also carries conformance information under tcpMIBConformance, with a set of compliance statements and a set of object groups. The compliance statement notes that a number of INDEX objects cannot be created or modified, and describes which groups a conforming implementation must support.
sections.plainLanguage: The listener table says which ports a device is waiting on and which program is waiting there. It records a wildcard listener in three different ways, depending on whether the program takes IPv4, IPv6 or both.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are a number of management objects defined in this MIB module with a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write. Such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments, and support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. The tcpConnectionState and tcpConnState objects are read-write, which allows termination of an arbitrary connection, so unauthorized access could cause a denial of service.

Some readable objects may also be sensitive. The connection tables contain information about the active connections on the device, their status and the associated processes; that information may be used by an attacker to launch attacks against known or unknown weaknesses in certain protocols and applications, and access to the connection table could have privacy implications because it provides detailed information on active connections. The listener tables contain information about listeners on an entity, for example the local port objects, which can be used to identify what ports are open on the machine and what attacks are likely to succeed, without the attacker having to run a port scanner.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Even if the network itself is secure, there is no control over who on that network may GET or SET the objects in this module. It is RECOMMENDED that implementers consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and that deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Two risks stand out. Anyone who can write the state column can cut connections, and anyone who can read the tables learns which ports are open and which programs own them, which saves an attacker from scanning. The RFC therefore asks for SNMPv3 with encryption and authentication.

items.label: listen
items.desc: Included only for parallelism with the old table; do not use.

items.label: synSent
items.desc: The connection has sent a SYN and is waiting.

items.label: synReceived
items.desc: The SYN was received and a SYN-ACK was sent.

items.label: finWait1
items.desc: The local side has closed and is waiting for the FIN to be acknowledged.

items.label: finWait2
items.desc: The FIN was acknowledged; waiting for the remote side to close.

items.label: closeWait
items.desc: The remote side closed; the local side has not closed yet.

items.label: lastAck
items.desc: The local side closed and is waiting for the final acknowledgement.

items.label: closing
items.desc: Both sides closed at the same time.

items.label: timeWait
items.desc: Waiting out the close so that old segments cannot confuse the connection.

items.label: deleteTCB
items.desc: The only value a manager may write; it deletes the connection.
